title: In 63,046 human genomes, 1-10 kb deletions of 512-2,047 conserved non-coding bases are about as rare as coding deletions in weakly constrained genes; non-conserved regulatory DNA matters less
abstract: In 63,046 human genomes, natural deletions of 1-10 kb that remove 512-2,047 non-coding bases conserved across mammals are about as rare as deletions of coding sequence in weakly constrained genes, while deletions that remove the same amount of non-conserved regulatory DNA are less rare, by a factor of about 2.5 to 50 that the data cannot fix. This matters because the dispute about how much of the genome is functional depends on whether biochemically active but non-conserved DNA matters for fitness; a deletion removes whole elements, so it tests function independently of conservation and of point mutations. We used 456,518 high-quality deletions (50 bp to 100 kb) from gnomAD v4.1 structural variants. Purifying selection keeps harmful deletions rare, so it increases the fraction of singletons (deletions seen in one person). In four size bands we compared deletions of the same size, caller, 1-Mb region, repeat and GC content, gene distance, aligned fraction, weakly conserved content and breakpoint repeat type, and we fitted several functional forms. Removing 512-2,047 conserved bases (Zoonomia phyloP >= 2.27) raised the singleton probability by 8.3 and 4.1 percentage points in 1-3.2 kb and 3.2-10 kb deletions, similar to coding deletions of genes with s_het < 0.01 (6.9 and 4.0) and below those of dosage-sensitive genes (11.1 and 9.2). Conserved bases outside ENCODE candidate cis-regulatory elements (cCREs) had effects at least as large as those inside. Non-conserved cCRE DNA had no consistent effect below about 500 bases and a smaller effect above (equal-amount ratio to conserved DNA 0.02-0.42; summary ratios 0.03-0.65 by band and form). Element-free DNA between 622 CRISPRi-validated enhancers and their genes was not rarer than such DNA at tested non-regulating pairs (50-249 bp deletions: +0.0 points, 95% CI -2.9 to 3.0), and element-free intronic DNA of dosage-sensitive genes was not rarer than other element-free DNA (-0.3, CI -1.2 to 0.6); these tests do not cover spacer deletions of 1 kb or more. lncRNA exons had no consistent effect beyond their conserved bases. The conserved dose response confirms, on a four-times larger callset, a graded relation reported for gnomAD-SV v2. Two independent reviews showed that our first summary (7%) depended on the model, so we report ranges. Limits: allele frequency is an indirect measure of selection, short-read SV calls have size-specific artifacts, and 10-100 kb deletions gave model-dependent results.
